Ontario senior homeowners’ property tax grant: up to CAD 500, how it can shrink the OEPTC, and why an extra RRIF dollar can cost 5.33 cents more

Work out the 2026 Ontario senior homeowners’ property tax grant from 2025 income and property tax, see when CRA’s Step 5 cuts the senior energy and property tax credit because of it, and price what a larger withdrawal costs in lost grant and credit. Includes how far CAD 500, unchanged since 2010, has fallen behind Ontario prices.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 27 October 2026 · 9 min read
Sources reviewed 27 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Ontario senior homeowners’ property tax grant beside the senior OEPTC: what a homeowner aged 64 or older receives, when the grant reduces the credit, and what extra income costs

Interactive planning lab

2026 senior homeowners’ property tax grant (one payment)$266.9
2026 OEPTC before Step 5 (Step 4)$1,153.18
OEPTC removed by Step 5 because of the grant$0
2026 OEPTC after Step 5 (paid with the Ontario trillium benefit)$1,153.18
Grant and OEPTC together$1,420.08

Share of the extra income lost to tax and the two payments25.33%

For a single senior aged 64 or older with $42,000 of 2025 adjusted net income and $3,600 of 2025 property tax, the 2026 grant is $266.90 (the lesser of CAD 500 and the tax, less 3.33% of income over $35,000) and the OEPTC is $1,153.18 before Step 5. Step 5 removes nothing: the grant and the credit together stay below your property tax plus the energy component. Together: $1,420.08. Adding $5,000 of income would cost $166.50 of grant and $100.00 of OEPTC, plus $1,000 of tax at the assumed 20%, leaving $3,734. Estimates from Ontario and CRA rules for the 2026 grant and the July 2026 to June 2027 OEPTC; the Ontario sales tax credit, the Northern Ontario energy credit, rent, long-term care and federal benefits that also depend on income are not included.

The central idea

An Ontario homeowner aged 64 or older on 31 December 2025 can get a 2026 grant of up to CAD 500, never more than the 2025 property tax, reduced by 3.33% of adjusted net income over CAD 35,000 (single) or CAD 45,000 (couple) and nil at CAD 50,000 or 60,000. It is paid once, tax-free, about four to eight weeks after the 2025 notice of assessment. It reduces the senior OEPTC only when the two together would exceed the property tax plus the energy component, which happens only with small property tax bills. Where both are being reduced, each extra dollar of 2025 income costs 5.33 cents of the two payments before any income tax. At Ontario prices, CAD 500 in 2025 bought what about CAD 352 did in 2010.

01

A small grant that sits beside a larger credit

Ontario has two separate payments that help seniors with property tax. The Ontario senior homeowners’ property tax grant (OSHPTG) is at most CAD 500 and is paid once a year. The Ontario energy and property tax credit (OEPTC) is part of the Ontario trillium benefit and, for someone 64 or older, can reach CAD 1,488 for July 2026 to June 2027. Both are claimed on the same form, ON-BEN, with the 2025 return, and both depend on 2025 income.

That raises three planning questions for a retired homeowner: how much the grant is, whether receiving it reduces the credit, and what an extra dollar of 2025 income — a larger RRIF withdrawal, a capital gain, a part-time job — costs in the two payments together. The calculator answers all three. Its default is a single senior with CAD 42,000 of adjusted net income and CAD 3,600 of property tax, weighing CAD 5,000 more income.

02

The grant: who qualifies and how much

According to the Government of Ontario and CRA’s questions and answers, you can apply for the 2026 grant on your 2025 return if, on 31 December 2025, you were at least 64, resident in Ontario, and you or your spouse or common-law partner owned and occupied your principal residence, with Ontario property tax paid for 2025. Holders of a life lease, or a lease of 10 years or more, can also qualify. The amount is:

Single, separated, divorced or widowedMarried or common-law
MaximumThe lesser of CAD 500 and the eligible property tax paid for 2025
Full maximum up toCAD 35,000 of adjusted net incomeCAD 45,000 of adjusted family net income
Reduction above that3.33% of the income over the threshold
No grant fromCAD 50,000CAD 60,000

At 3.33%, CAD 15,000 of income over the threshold removes CAD 499.50, so the grant ends almost exactly where the cut-off is. Only one person in a couple can receive it. If only one spouse was 64 or older, that spouse must apply for both, and the same spouse must also apply for the couple’s OEPTC and Northern Ontario energy credit. The grant is non-taxable. CRA says it is paid about four to eight weeks after the notice of assessment.

The property tax that counts is the tax actually paid for 2025 on the principal residence. A couple living together enters the total for both of them; someone who co-owns with a person other than a spouse enters only their own share; someone who moved enters the tax for each home for the time they lived there. Deferred tax that was not paid does not count.

03

When the grant reduces the OEPTC: CRA’s Step 5

CRA’s 2026 OEPTC calculation sheets for seniors work in five steps. For a homeowner with no rent, the occupancy cost (Step 1) is the 2025 property tax. The energy component (Step 2) is that cost up to CAD 290. The property tax component (Step 3) is CAD 617 plus 10% of the cost, the 10% capped at CAD 581, and never more than the cost itself. Step 4 adds the two and subtracts 2% of adjusted family net income over CAD 36,309 (single) or CAD 43,571 (couple).

Step 5 applies only to someone who receives the grant. It adds the grant to the Step 4 credit, subtracts the energy component and then the property tax, and takes whatever is left off the credit. In plain terms: the grant and the OEPTC together cannot exceed the property tax plus the energy component. CRA’s questions and answers put the same test as the property tax component plus the grant exceeding the property tax paid, and add that for most seniors the grant does not affect the credit.

Single senior, CAD 30,000 incomeProperty tax CAD 300CAD 1,000CAD 2,000CAD 3,600
GrantCAD 300CAD 500CAD 500CAD 500
OEPTC before Step 5CAD 590CAD 1,007CAD 1,107CAD 1,267
Removed by Step 5CAD 300CAD 217CAD 0CAD 0
Grant and OEPTC togetherCAD 590CAD 1,290CAD 1,607CAD 1,767

With CAD 1,000 of tax the cap is CAD 1,000 + CAD 290 = CAD 1,290, so CAD 217 of the credit goes. From about CAD 1,242 of tax at this income there is no reduction, because the property tax component (CAD 617 plus 10%) then grows more slowly than the tax itself. A higher income lowers Step 4 first, which pushes the point where Step 5 bites lower still.

04

The 5.33% band on extra income

Both payments fall as 2025 income rises, but from different starting points. For a single senior the OEPTC falls by 2% of income over CAD 36,309, and the grant by 3.33% over CAD 35,000. Between CAD 36,309 and CAD 50,000 both are falling, so every extra dollar of 2025 income costs 5.33 cents of the two payments, before any income tax. For a couple the overlap runs from CAD 45,000 to CAD 60,000. Below the thresholds, and once the grant has gone, only the 2% applies, until the OEPTC itself is used up.

Single senior, CAD 3,600 property taxGrantOEPTCTogether

CAD 49,999CAD 0.53CAD 993.20CAD 993.73

CAD 60,000CAD 0CAD 793.18CAD 793.18

These are small amounts next to income tax, but they stack with other income-tested amounts that the calculator does not include: the Ontario sales tax credit, the federal age amount, the GIS for lower incomes, and OAS recovery tax for much higher ones. Adjusted family net income for a couple is the two net incomes added together, so either spouse’s extra income has the same effect. Pension income splitting moves income between spouses but does not change the total.

05

Four worked cases

  1. The default. A single senior with CAD 42,000 of adjusted net income and CAD 3,600 of property tax. Grant: CAD 500 − 3.33% × CAD 7,000 = CAD 266.90. OEPTC: CAD 290 + CAD 977 − 2% × CAD 5,691 = CAD 1,153.18. Step 5 removes nothing, because CAD 1,420.08 is well below CAD 3,600 + CAD 290. Together: CAD 1,420.08.
  2. CAD 5,000 more RRIF income. At CAD 47,000 the grant is CAD 100.40 and the OEPTC CAD 1,053.18: CAD 266.50 less, exactly 5.33% of CAD 5,000. With income tax assumed at 20%, CAD 3,733.50 of the CAD 5,000 is left, an effective 25.33%.
  3. A small tax bill. A single senior with CAD 30,000 of income and CAD 1,000 of property tax: grant CAD 500, OEPTC CAD 1,007 before Step 5. Step 5 removes CAD 217, leaving CAD 790; the two together are CAD 1,290, the tax plus CAD 290.
  4. A couple. CAD 55,000 of adjusted family net income and CAD 4,800 of property tax: grant CAD 500 − 3.33% × CAD 10,000 = CAD 167; OEPTC CAD 290 + CAD 1,097 − 2% × CAD 11,429 = CAD 1,158.42. Only one spouse receives the grant and the credit, on behalf of both.

An independent 40-digit decimal check reproduces every figure above and in the tables, and the tests check that the grant never exceeds CAD 500 or the property tax, is nil at the cut-offs, that the two payments together never exceed the property tax plus the energy component when a grant is received, and that neither ever rises with income.

06

CAD 500 since 2010, in Ontario prices

CRA states that the maximum grant has been CAD 500 for 2010 and later years. Statistics Canada’s annual consumer price index for Ontario (all items, 2002=100) was 116.5 in 2010 and 165.6 in 2025, an increase of 42.1%. The restated amounts below are calculations from those two observations:

Amount in the grant rulesSame purchasing power in 2025 prices
CAD 500 maximumCAD 711
CAD 35,000 single thresholdCAD 49,751
CAD 45,000 couple thresholdCAD 63,966

Neither the Ontario nor the CRA page describes any indexation of the grant amounts, while the OEPTC amounts are changed each benefit year. One consequence: a retiree whose income only keeps pace with prices drifts further into the grant’s reduction band each year, and fewer seniors qualify at all. Whether the amounts will change is a policy decision; the chart only shows what has happened to their purchasing power so far.

07

Claiming it and planning around it

  1. File, and complete ON-BEN. The grant is applied for on the 2025 return by entering the property tax paid on line 61120 of Form ON-BEN, even if you have no income to report. CRA says late applications for recent years can be made by asking for an adjustment of the return.
  2. In a couple, choose the right applicant. The applicant must be 64 or older if only one spouse is, and the same person claims the OEPTC and NOEC for both.
  3. Check the size of the property tax. Step 5 can only reduce the OEPTC when the tax bill is small: below about CAD 1,242 for anyone with the full CAD 500 grant, and lower still at higher incomes. That is more likely after a property tax deferral, in a small or rural home, or for a share of a jointly owned property.
  4. Look at withdrawals across years. Inside the 5.33% band, a one-off withdrawal or gain in 2025 lowers the 2026 grant and OEPTC; the same amount spread over several years may stay below the thresholds. RRIF minimums cannot be reduced, and income tax usually matters more, so treat this as one input, not the reason for a withdrawal plan.
  5. Plan the cash. The grant arrives once, after assessment; the OEPTC is paid monthly from 10 July 2026, or in one payment if the year’s trillium benefit is CAD 500 or less, or in June 2027 if you chose to wait.

08

What the calculator leaves out

  • Other parts of the trillium benefit. The Ontario sales tax credit and the Northern Ontario energy credit are not shown; see the related trillium benefit guide.
  • Other housing. Rent, long-term care, reserve energy costs, student residences, mobile homes on leased land and a move during the year are not modelled. Single seniors with a child use different OEPTC sheets.
  • Eligibility. Age, residence and ownership on 31 December 2025, and the confinement rule, are assumed to be met.
  • Rounding. CRA’s own rounding and minimum payment rules are not applied to the grant.
  • The tax rate. It is an editable assumption, not a calculation of federal and Ontario tax, credits and clawbacks.
  • Future years. Only the 2026 grant and the July 2026 to June 2027 OEPTC amounts are used.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 27 October 2026. The fourth chart uses Statistics Canada’s annual Ontario consumer price index (table 18-10-0005-01, 2010 to 2025, released 19 January 2026), an observation; the restated amounts are calculations. The other four apply the Government of Ontario’s grant rules (page updated 2 January 2026), CRA’s OSHPTG questions and answers (page details 20 January 2026) and CRA’s 2026 senior OEPTC calculation sheets (page details 30 July 2026), reviewed 27 October 2026, to hypothetical editable households: a homeowner, or a couple, aged 64 or older with no children, no rent, no long-term care costs and no reserve energy costs. The Ontario sales tax credit, the Northern Ontario energy credit and federal income-tested benefits are not included. These are planning estimates, not CRA’s determination.
